t: Make the XOR of All Segments Equal to Zero — Periodicity Shrinks Windows Into Residue Classes
o:
## Understanding the problem

We may overwrite array entries (values must stay below 2¹⁰) so that every contiguous window of length k has XOR zero, minimizing the number of changed positions. Compare adjacent windows W(s) = nums[s..s+k−1] and W(s+1): their XORs differ exactly by nums[s] ⊕ nums[s+k]. If all windows are zero, then nums[s] ⊕ nums[s+k] = 0 for every valid s — the array must be **periodic with period k** — and additionally W(0) itself must XOR to zero. Conversely, periodicity plus a zero first window forces every window to zero. So the problem becomes: make each residue class i mod k constant (paying 1 per changed position) such that the k class constants XOR to zero.

**Example walkthrough:** with k = 1 the condition collapses to every element being 0, so [1,2,0,3,0] costs 3 changes. For [3,4,5,2,1,7,3,4,7] with k = 3 the classes keep majority values 3, 4, 7 — and indeed 3 ⊕ 4 ⊕ 7 = 0 — costing one change per class, 3 total. For [1,2,4,1,2,5,1,2,6] the majorities 1, 2, 6 fail the checksum, so one class switches its constant wholesale; the answer is still 3.

With n ≤ 2000 but values ranging over 2¹⁰ possibilities, the joint checksum suggests a knapsack-style DP whose state is the running XOR of chosen class constants — only 1024 states.
k: All size-k windows XOR to zero if and only if nums[i] = nums[i+k] for every valid i AND the first window XORs to zero — periodicity plus one checksum.
Partition indices by i mod k: each class must become one repeated value, and the k class values must XOR to 0.
Values live in [0, 2^10), so a DP over the running XOR (1024 states) captures the cross-class constraint exactly.
Rewriting an entire class costs its size and can realize ANY target value — a universal fallback transition that keeps the DP feasible everywhere.

a.n: Approach 1: Residue classes + DP over the running XOR
a.i: For each residue class j record its size and value frequencies, and let dp[j][x] be the minimum changes using classes 0..j so their constants XOR to x. Transition per class: either keep some value v occurring c times (pay size − c, move state x to x ⊕ v), or rewrite the whole class arbitrarily (pay size, reach any state — encoded compactly as size + min(previous dp)). Enumerating only values that actually occur in the class bounds the work by Σ(distinct values per class) · 1024 ≤ n · 2^10 ≈ 2·10⁶. The answer sits at dp after the last class, state 0.
s: Bucket positions by i mod k; tally per-class frequencies and sizes.
Initialize dp[0] = 0 (empty prefix, XOR state 0) and every other state to infinity.
For each class j, seed ndp[x] = size_j + min(dp) — the rewrite-the-whole-class fallback.
For each occurring value v with count c, relax ndp[x] = min(ndp[x], dp[x ⊕ v] + size_j − c) over all states x.
After processing all k classes return dp[0].
a.t: O(n · 2^10) — each occurrence yields one kept-value per class, expanded against at most 1024 DP states
a.sp: O(k · 2^10) — frequency tables per class plus two 1024-slot DP rows

## Wrap-up

This is a reduction problem wearing a DP costume. Nail the adjacent-windows observation out loud — interviewers weight it heavily — and the residue-class DP becomes standard fare.

**Common pitfalls**

- Missing the rewrite-whole-class fallback transition: cases like example 3 where the majority values fail the XOR checksum become unsolvable without it.
- Wrong initialization: before any class, only XOR state 0 is reachable, at cost 0 — not every state at cost 0.
- Sentinel too small: total changes can reach n = 2000, so an "infinity" of 1024 breaks comparisons; use something safely above n.
- Trailing partial blocks (n not divisible by k): the last incomplete window imposes no checksum, but periodicity still applies — both the derivation and the code above handle this automatically since the first window always exists.

**Likely follow-ups:** reconstruct which positions were changed; generalize to windows of size at most k; or discuss why the 2^10 value bound is essential to this complexity.
